Rebuilding an Axolotl Limb

When an axolotl loses part of a limb, the animal can rebuild bone, muscle, skin, nerves, and blood vessels. The replacement does not appear all at once. It develops through an ordered sequence of cellular changes.

Covered by a new layer of cells, protection forms over the wound.[1] Beneath that covering, cells gather into a mass called a blastema. Chemical signals help cells respond to their location, so tissue near a wrist does not organize as though it were near a shoulder.[2]

The blastema explodes[3] as its cells divide. Some cells contribute to new muscle, while others rebuild cartilage and connective tissue. A network of nerves and growing blood vessels support[4] the developing limb. Over time, the new structures take on the proportions and arrangement appropriate to the missing section.

Regeneration is therefore not the same as simply producing more cells. Growth must be coordinated across several tissues and along the correct spatial pattern. Studying that coordination may help researchers understand why other vertebrates usually repair major injuries with scars instead of rebuilding complete structures.[5]
